text: A dashboard from Lesson 21 only helps if someone's actually looking at it. A CloudWatch Alarm removes that requirement entirely — it watches one metric continuously and fires the moment it crosses a threshold you define, with no one needing to be staring at a chart when it happens, day or night, weekday or weekend.

Every alarm is built from the same pieces: the metric to watch, a statistic like Average or Maximum, a period measured in seconds, and a comparison operator with a threshold. CPUUtilization above 80% for 5 minutes becomes a 300-second period with one evaluation period breaching it — set once with put-metric-alarm, pointed at an instance by its dimensions, and it runs forever after with no further attention needed.

An alarm isn't simply on or off. It lives in one of three states: OK, where the metric is within bounds; ALARM, where the threshold has been breached for the configured evaluation periods; and INSUFFICIENT_DATA, which is normal right after an instance first launches, before enough data points exist to judge anything. Only the transition into ALARM actually fires a notification.

An alarm doesn't send an email itself — it publishes to an SNS topic, and SNS, Simple Notification Service, fans that out to every subscriber on it: an email address, a phone number for SMS, or an HTTP webhook endpoint. One real gotcha catches people off guard — a brand-new email or SMS subscription sits pending confirmation until that person clicks the confirmation link AWS sends them. Skip that step, and the alarm can fire exactly on schedule while that subscriber hears nothing at all.

Create the topic, subscribe an address, have them confirm it, then attach the topic's ARN to the alarm's actions — in that order, or the notification goes nowhere. Next, Lesson 23 covers where the detailed records behind all of this actually live: CloudWatch Logs and the log groups that organize them.
